title: The crust was stretched thin and should have subsided, yet the American West rose a mile
dek: Evidence of plate stretching is usually buried by sediment; the Basin and Range Province in the US is a rare exception: the crust has been extended to about twice its original width and is still stretching, and GPS, paleoseismic records, and detachment faults let us see it.
why: The opening introduction lays out the most anomalous core of the Basin and Range Province in one go: it has been stretched to twice its width, it is still moving, GPS can measure it in real time, and rocks from 15 km depth have been brought to the surface. It works as a condensed guide to Basin and Range research.
who: Graduate students in structural geology, GPS crustal deformation observers, and physical geography enthusiasts who want to quickly grasp why the Basin and Range differs from compressional orogens.

points.h: Evidence of stretching is almost always buried by sediment
points.body: The result of plate collision is clear: the edges are crumpled and thrown up into mountain belts. But when plates are stretched, the evidence is usually lost. The loss chain has two steps: the thinned lithosphere subsides, and the basins formed by subsidence are then filled with sediment. So the surface is left with only a flat cover, showing no sign of the earlier rifting. The opening uses this contrast to set up the episode's suspense—if you want to study extension, you must find a window like the Basin and Range that has not been erased by sediment.

points.h: Dozens of parallel ranges were not squeezed out by compression
points.body: The Basin and Range is called a great exception in the original: this region in the western US and northwestern Mexico, sandwiched between the Colorado Plateau and the Sierra Nevada, has dozens of ranges aligned nearly parallel, trending north. They are not isolated peaks but the surface relief left after the entire crust was lengthened. The distances and arrangement indicate that what happened here was not one compression but a large-scale extension. Because it retains a complete basin-and-range topography, it is a natural laboratory for studying the extension process.

points.h: The crust has been stretched to twice its width, and it is still stretching
points.body: The episode gives a hard number: the crust of the Basin and Range has been extended to about twice its original width. This is not a static ancient relic, because the description is immediately followed by 'still stretching today'—it is still widening today. The stretching rate is invisible to the naked eye, but the scale is enough to change the region's overall topography. The factor of two determines its geological significance, while 'reaching today' turns it from a historical problem into a dynamic problem that can be monitored in real time.

points.h: GPS antennas can measure in real time that the West is widening
points.body: The episode lists three sources of evidence for extension: first, GPS antennas fixed to bedrock, which can measure in real time that the Basin and Range is widening; second, paleoseismic records, which preserve the history of faulting events caused by extension; and third, dismembered thrust sheets, which allow researchers to reassemble the entire region as it was 20 million years ago. The three have different time scales: GPS looks at the present, seismic records look at geological history, and thrust sheets look at regional-scale paleostructure. Only by combining them can one conclude that the crust has been stretched to twice its width.

points.h: Rocks from 15 km depth can be exposed without erosion
points.body: Low-angle detachment faults are the most counterintuitive structure in this passage. One of their major functions is to bring rocks from 15 km depth to the surface—not by wholesale uplift of the range, but by sliding along a low-angle fault surface and detaching. Fifteen kilometers depth roughly corresponds to the middle-upper crust, where rocks would take an extremely long time to be exposed by erosion; detachment faults provide a more direct path. Being able to see deep rocks directly is key to understanding the internal structure of the extension process.

points.h: The thinned crust should have collapsed, but it did not
points.body: The episode ends by flipping the question to topography: since the crust of the Basin and Range has been thinned, why does it still stand at about a mile high? Common sense says rifting corresponds to subsidence, but here the plateau has not collapsed. The opening introduction only poses this paradox without giving an answer, clearly a hook for the main interview. For an extensional province, the coexistence of high elevation and thinned crust is itself a fact that needs explanation.

terms.def: A large region of crustal extension in the western US and northwestern Mexico, characterized by alternating parallel mountain ranges and basins.
The process by which the crust is lengthened and thinned under tensional stress.
Large normal faults with a gentle dip that can bring deep crustal rocks to shallow levels.
Rock bodies emplaced by thrusting that have subsequently been broken and offset by extension and block faulting.

quotes.text: But where a plate is stretched rather than squeezed, the evidence is usually lost, because the thinned lithosphere subsides and the basins that form fill with sediment.
The Basin and Range Province of the western United States and northwestern Mexico is the great exception.

Between the Colorado Plateau and the Sierra Nevada, dozens of mountain ranges march north in near-parallel array, in a crust that has been pulled out to about twice its original width — and it is still stretching today.

In this episode we look at how we know that: from GPS antennas bolted into bedrock that measure the province widening in real time, to the record of ancient earthquakes, to the dismembered thrust sheets that let the whole region be reassembled as it was 20 million years ago.
We also discuss the low-angle detachment faults that have brought rock from fifteen kilometres down up to the surface and why a stretched province still stands a mile high.
